speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members have filed a number of Parliamentary Questions on the topic of fair employment practices – some are for the next Sitting and others are for Written Answers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I appreciate that these questions are of concern to Singaporeans and seek Members' understanding to take these related questions together, so that we can deal with them more holistically.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Foo Mee Har asked how employers’ employment practices are monitored and employers held accountable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked about tripartite discussions on discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In practice, MOM works closely with the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices or TAFEP to follow up on all complaints of potential malpractices at workplaces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All forms of discrimination are covered, including for age, gender, ethnicity and family circumstances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also monitor the workforce profiles of firms for potential unfair hiring practices against Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means that the company cannot renew existing work passes or have new applications approved – some for as long as two years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These penalties are serious and the employers know it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To stay in business, it will be necessary for them to boost local employment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Employment Pass or EP applications from these firms are held back, while TAFEP engages these firms to help them improve their human resource practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Louis Chua suggested publicly naming firms placed on the FCF Watchlist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chua further asked for these firms’ access to Government grants and tax incentives schemes to be withdrawn.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I explained in Parliament on 1 September 2020, unlike firms whom we have taken to task for infringements, firms on the FCF Watchlist have not flouted any rules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members may recall that on Tuesday, I shared a few examples.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Upon investigation, we found some employers to be genuinely unfamiliar with local recruitment channels or whose recruitment had been limited by directives imposed by overseas headquarters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Measures we take for these firms must therefore be proportional and also consider the impact on their existing local workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In most instances, employers on the FCF Watchlist have been responsive to TAFEP’s engagement efforts and expanded their employment of local PMETs with help from Workforce Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Naming these firms would likely have frustrated their local hiring efforts and is ultimately counter-productive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, following TAFEP’s intervention, many firms exit the FCF Watchlist within a year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the minority who are uncooperative, refusing to make adjustments even after options have been suggested to them, their work pass privileges remain suspended.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In all, 3,200 EP applications by these employers have been rejected or withheld by MOM, or withdrawn subsequently by the firms themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we withheld 3,200 or rejected them, or they got withdrawn.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And then, these firms collectively hired more than 4,800 Singaporean PMETs in total.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This comes on top of all the local employees that these firms originally employed and continued to retain.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We plan to proactively engage even more companies under the FCF, such as those whose Singaporean Core has been weakening, or whose EP and S Pass workforce are concentrated with a single foreign nationality source.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will work with economic agencies like EDB and MAS to engage these firms to improve their workforce profiles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also engage the HR community to do more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Whether or not the firms are on the FCF Watchlist, where MOM has found evidence of discriminatory hiring practices, we have taken the companies to task and publicised the names of these firms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In January 2020, MOM released the names of four employers penalised for pre-selection of foreigners or not adhering to the spirit of the FCF job advertising requirement, and one employer for gender-related discriminatory hiring.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In March 2020, MOM released the names of five employers penalised for age-related discriminatory hiring.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is no different than if the company had been charged in Court for employment offences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On Ms He Ting Ru’s question, tripartite consultations in recent months have focused on ensuring fairness when companies implement cost-saving measures or have to retrench workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, on cost-saving measures, the National Wages Council or NWC was convened in March this year and was re-convened in August.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is expected to update guidelines on managing excess manpower within this month.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Since March this year, MOM has introduced a new requirement for employers to notify MOM of their cost-saving measures.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Ms Foo Mee Har’s question, we identify companies whose notifications are concerning and TAFEP engages them to assess whether their measures are fair and reasonable.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similarly, we mediated another 1,000 or so complaints by employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, on retrenchments, MOM, NTUC and the Singapore National Employers Federation jointly updated the Tripartite Advisory on Managing Excess Manpower and Responsible Retrenchment or TAMEM in March.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, this retrenchment requirement would already have covered about 90% of the workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through the notification regime, we actively monitor retrenchment practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Vast majority of the retrenchments have been conducted fairly and responsibly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Firms that have not done so fairly will be investigated and MOM may take strong enforcement actions such as suspending their work pass privileges.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nonetheless, we encourage these firms to still notify MOM, so that Workforce Singapore, the tripartite partners and other relevant agencies can step in promptly to provide job assistance to affected employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also expanded outreach efforts to jobseekers, so that retrenched workers may get help even if their employers did not notify MOM.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM and our tripartite partners will continue to guard against unfair hiring or retrenchment practices and take appropriate action against errant employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could I ask how many of these companies are there because of discrimination against women and on family responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, on the earlier suggestion that I made this week, on whether we can legislate these guidelines on fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think it makes a bit of sense.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you discriminate against Singaporeans and hire foreigners, we will restrict or curtail your work pass privileges; we do not allow you to hire foreigners.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This conversation seems very intimate, with both of you standing there, across each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, a point of clarification that the Member sought, which are the 1,200 companies that we had scrutinised over the years under FCF, what kinds of concerns did we have.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I explained, they had not made any infringements.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In general, we found that there was a heavier proportion of foreigners in their PMET workforce, compared to their industry peers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we picked them up and tried to undersand why their workforce profiles were the way they were, and helped them to improve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Member has asked whether for other forms of discrimination – not nationality discrimination but for other forms of discrimination – whether legislation is the right tool and we could consider that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If I can cite the example of concerns about age discrimination.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do have the Retirement and Re-employment Act which stipulates the minimum age below which employers cannot say, "You're too old and you must retire." We also have the re-employment age legislation which compels the employers, even after his employee has reached the minimum statutory retirement age, to offer re-employment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So that we safeguard the opportunities for them to continue working – not necessarily in the same job and not necessarily holding the same pay.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Using legislative tools in order to protect the interest of workers is not so unthinkable and have been used on many different occasions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I understand where the Member is coming from, that in terms of legislating against discrimination for gender, should we perhaps take the next step forward.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have also responded to – I am sorry, I should have done this another way – I texted Mr Vikram Nair after he gave his speech yesterday.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I will share with Members what I texted him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He gave the suggestion that perhaps you can provide legislative levers to allow individuals who had been aggrieved by nationality bias to seek redress from the employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The crux here really is that if you speak to all the women, yes, on occasions, we have identified cases where the employers, either the questions that they asked were very biased, in terms of suggesting that their family circumstances were not welcome at the workplace, or that the very fact that they were women prevented them from doing certain roles.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We know of some employers like that, but they are very much in the minority.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You will also see that there are many women who have gotten into good positions because their employers are quite enlightened.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It basically can be quite prescriptive in nature.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What else it is that we have done to promote women in employment and make sure that they get a fair deal?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have, for example, through many years of investment in their education, helped them to acquire the skills no different from men, and they can advance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the other one that we have always been very mindful of, and women Members of Parliament have spoken on this extensively, it has to do with how you can improve the support that they have from the family, so that does not prevent them from making progress in their careers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The first one is, I hear from the Minister that some companies have directives from their HQ out of Singapore to ask them to practise unfair recruitment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Why can we not nip the problem at source where we inform the companies before they set up shop in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And number two, we have also heard the Minister said they do surveillance and identify companies that have a high concentration of Employment and S Pass holders, all from certain a nationality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Can MOM be even more proactive even before they have this number that is of concern?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Can you stop them from hiring anymore workers based on S Pass and E Pass, which means it is more proactive than after the fact itself?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The third one is that I would like the Minister to consider what I said in my speech on Monday, to set up a National Human Resource Committee, so that you have regular engagement with the head of human resources and personnel in the various large companies, to share with them the best practices on how to form a Singaporean Core.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What they did, however, not recognise or did not understand our employment landscape, was that actually many of the positions that they were seeking do not necessarily require degree qualifications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, if they are seeking an IT role, actually our Polytechnic graduates are just as qualified, and with the right training can also do the job.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, what the local office previously did was blindly implement the directive from the headquarters that every single one of their recruits must meet degree qualifications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When we pointed out to them that for the positions that they are hiring, Polytechnic diploma holders are equally qualified, what they then did was to take it up with headquarters and persuaded the headquarters to change the recruitment criteria.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the Member Mr Ang's suggestion on the National Human Resource Committee, it already exists.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is called the Institute of Human Resource Professionals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We engage them regularly and we intend to do more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then there are other similar organisations, the Singapore Human Resource Institute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are also very active in trying to level up HR practices in Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think they do really want to help and raise the bar, and we very much encourage their proactive efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The first is, the Minister mentioned that most of the companies exit this watchlist after a year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I would like to know how many persistent offenders have we seen amongst the companies who have been on the watchlist.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because this will inform us as to whether the sanctions are enough.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I think this is helpful information for us to know.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And second is the balance of complaints and active surveillance that has been conducted by MOM.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The third is whether there are any GLCs who are currently on the watchlist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the Member wanted to know whether we have put any Temasek-linked companies on the watchlist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second question, is the balance between complaints and proactive surveillance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Actually, the proactive surveillance has brought us into more direct engagements with the companies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: None of these companies would have been surfaced to our attention if not for proactive surveillance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their employees actually did not raise the concerns with us.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you look at the complaints that were raised to MOM and the number of companies that we have scrutinised, I do not have the exact figure with me, but based on my impression also getting emails and reading all the complaints that were filed with our Labour Relations Department, I stand corrected, but actually I think our proactive surveillance has reached out to more companies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The reason why I do not give you a very specific number is because even if the company has exited from the watchlist, it does not mean we stop watching them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If they revert to the old patterns of hiring and we are concerned about their workforce profile again, then they can get put back into the watchlist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And, Sir, if I may, I should also answer Mr Ang's earlier question.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He said why not take an even more proactive approach.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I also said in my reply that we intend to engage an even wider group of companies to reshape their workforce profiles.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have two supplementary questions in two areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The second question, on the mandatory reporting of retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the area of FCF, I have suggested of us publishing and, of course, many Members of this House as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: If there are companies that have been recalcitrant, meaning after one year of rehabilitation or assistance, they have not improved, is there a problem publicising this list of recalcitrant employers?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Because, if you see many of the malpractices, the lay-offs that are happening in the past couple of months, mostly are from micro-SMEs and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: From two perspectives: one, we want to ensure fair retrenchment practices; two, we want to ensure we provide the necessary interventions from Workforce Singapore as well e2i, to assist some of these micro-SMEs and SMEs, so that we have advanced and proactive or pre-emptive steps that we can take to help these companies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So, from that perspective, I hope MOM can look at both these areas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Just a gentle reminder to Members, please keep to your side of the Chamber.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Please keep to your side of the Chamber.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To ask every single one of them to make a report, even if most of them have not done anything bad prima facie, we are saying that we are not very sure, and it does not matter whether we can really pick it up much from it or not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I think we have to balance between whether we assume that every single one of them have retrenched in a very unfair manner and that is why the reporting will allow us to go after every single one of them, or do we ask whether there are complementary avenues.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, the two are complementary to each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not that we only need to depend on one tool.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On his other question about the FCF watchlist, whether the recalcitrant ones can be named, ultimately, it goes back to what our objective is.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If our objective is still to try and get them to improve their HR practices, what is a more effective way of doing so?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And you do not even need to name them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They find that this set of conditions is not what they would like to deal with; we accept that.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She mentioned in her speech that of the companies in the FCF framework, some were unfamiliar with MOM regulations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are a good spread, across different industries, some large, some small.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The first is, on the firms that had been taken to task, following being on the FCF watchlist.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the whole-of-Government level, has there been any correlation to see if these firms previously had been awarded tenders or contracts for Government or Government-related projects, and subsequent to being taken to task, whether any such firms subsequently were awarded Government tenders.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The second question is, whether as part of the paradigm of environmental, social and governance responsibility, which is increasingly being considered these days, whether some Government tenders can consider the role of HR practices either as a clear criterion or as a tie-breaker in the event of two companies having very similar value prepositions otherwise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just to briefly elaborate, the Mystery Shopper approach involves sending CVs with otherwise identical qualifications, but varying the age, the ethnicity as suggested by the name, to the company.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The idea is to, by doing this "A/B" testing to see whether there are companies that have a clear pattern of rejecting certain applications at the CV or resume stage.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This may help identify soft discrimination before it becomes a bigger issue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The proactive surveillance under FCF watchlist, is in fact, the "Mystery Shopper" programme that he has talked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These companies did not surface to our attention because their employees said that something was wrong.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Very similar to how Dr Tan has described it – a mixture of looking at their workforce profiles, a mixture of looking at how they have responded to advertisements that were put on MyCareersFuture.gov.sg.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You put the two together, we see that these companies in terms of their hiring patterns, something does not look quite right.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, then, we put them on the watchlist and we engage them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We asked what is going on, why is it that your pattern of recruitment has been like that?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is in substance, nearly identical, I think, to what Dr Tan has asked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think it goes back to what our objective really is.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What do you want as an outcome to for these companies that we have put on the watchlist?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is our objective that they improve their hiring so that more local PMETs can be added to their workforce?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Or is our objective to frustrate them and to somehow get them to exit Singapore or to exit the business, whatever it is that they are carrying on in Singapore?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Keep in mind that although we have identified these companies for proactive surveillance, for engagement, they also do have a sizable local PMET workforce.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are already hirers, employers of Singaporeans holding PMET positions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The actions that we take must be proportional and it must also not create so much difficulties for the existing PMETs in their workforce who are local and who would very much like to keep their jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, these are the things that we must keep in mind when we decide on what measures to take it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I am not saying that these measures will always be static.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we have a number of tools that we can use but all designed for one objective in mind, which is to reshape the workforce profiles of the companies and to ensure that they treat local candidates fairly, give them a chance to make progress in the companies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if these individuals have not been known to them, have not been on their radar for possible recruitment and training, then we would want them to make a special effort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first, is on the size of the TAFEP team that surveys, educates and takes action against companies that engage in unfair hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is the Minister of the view that that team needs to be enlarged?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question takes off from comments made by the Second Minister for Manpower in the course of the debate over the last few days.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Is MOM looking to beef up resources on unfair hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Could Minister share some details on what those measures specifically are?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have been beefing up, so the latest number I do not have it offhand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The answer is yes, but I would also say that at the same time, it is important for us to reach out to employers and to ensure that they do their part to upkeep fair hiring practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If all of our efforts are directed purely towards enforcement, I think what you do create as an environment is one where you are always pitted against each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You are always assuming that the employers are not trying to do their part, you are always assuming that the employers have something to hide and you are always assuming that the employers have no real difficulties that they are facing of their own.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you interact with enough employers, they will tell you that, "We have very serious challenges also in reaching out to potential jobseekers".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, we have to take a balanced approach and ask ourselves, what is the combination of actions that will be most helpful to the employers and to the businesses, which in turn will be more helpful to expanding opportunities for our own people.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That balance is one that we are always constantly trying to strike.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I was very cheered when Ms He Ting Ru asked the question of what are the tripartite discussions, the tripartite discussions are precisely this – how can each one of us do our part?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The unions are reaching out to the jobseekers, encouraging them to understand where the opportunities are and to be willing to be trained for those opportunities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The employers, being cognisant of the slack in the job market, in the availability of jobseekers, possibly redesigning their jobs so that more locals will be attracted to them and also making a real effort to participate in programmes that can help them to strengthen their local workforce.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I wonder what are the measures in place to deter employers from embedding the rental allowance or the kids education allowance into their salary to circumvent this regulation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think the answer is that, if the company was so inclined they can package the salary in any number of ways.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is not the spirit of what we are trying to pursue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And there are people who write to the MOM, they write in to me personally too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We take their feedback seriously, we follow up, we engage the company, we let them know that this has come to our attention, can you help us to understand what went on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If, in that process of engagement, we have reason to suspect that the companies are trying to do all kinds of things to avoid their obligations, to try to avoid good practices, then we will know what to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will have a bearing on their future applications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But we must wield this in a very smart way and not in a way that is detrimental to our own interests.
